title: The Serpent of Ambika Forest
subtitle: Nanda is swallowed and freed
story:
A cry cut through the Ambika forest in the small hours of the night, and every cowherd of Vraja woke at once. "Krishna! Krishna!" Nanda's voice rang through the trees. "A great serpent has taken me!"

There was no mistaking that voice, or the terror in it. The cowherds had come to the forest of the goddess Ambika to keep a vow, and they had lain down to sleep under the great trees, their cattle grazing at the edge of the clearing. Nanda, the chief of the herdsmen, slept at the centre of the camp — and when the cowherds came running with burning firebrands snatched from the campfire, they saw why he had cried out.

A serpent of impossible size lay coiled across the clearing, and Nanda was wrapped inside its folds. The creature had not eaten in a long time; hunger had driven it from the deep parts of the forest toward the sleeping men, and it had taken their leader like a mouse in a nest. It was already swallowing, its jaws working over Nanda's shoulders, and its coils tightened with every breath it drew.

The cowherds did not stop to think. They fell on the serpent together — beating it, scorching it, pressing the smoking ends of the firebrands into its scales, shouting all the while. The great snake shuddered and hissed; the smell of burning scales filled the clearing. But it did not let go. The fire that made the cowherds flinch back only made the serpent draw Nanda deeper, and Nanda's cries grew fainter as the great jaws worked.

Then Krishna came through the ring of desperate men. There was no weapon in his hand, no anger in his face. The cowherds fell back to let him pass, and he walked up to the serpent as if it were a stray calf, and touched it with his bare foot.

The touch undid what all their fire could not. The serpent released Nanda at once, its coils falling slack, and Nanda tumbled out onto the grass — shaken, breathless, alive. And where the monstrous body had lain, there now stood a being of molten light, as though the firebrands had finally taken hold and burned the beast away, leaving only what had been hidden inside it all along.

Krishna studied the radiant figure, which bowed low before him. "Who are you?" he asked. "You shine with a beauty that is wonderful to see."

"I was Sudarshana, a Vidyadhara," the being said, "one of the sky-farers. I was proud of my form and prouder still of my beauty, and one day I laughed at the sages of the Angirasa lineage to their faces. They cursed me — but theirs was a compassionate curse, laid on me as a grace I did not yet understand. It bound me in the body of this serpent, to crawl and to hunger until the touch of the blessed one should free me. That touch is yours, and this is the day. Your foot has burned away the evil of the curse, and I stand released."

"Then go," Krishna said. "The curse is finished."

Sudarshana praised him then — the one who takes away the fear of all who come to him for refuge, the great yogi, the lord of the good — and when his words ran out, he circled Krishna, bowed again at his feet, and rose into the dark sky until the night swallowed him.

The cowherds stood a long time in silence. The firebrands still smoked in their hands. Nanda sat on the grass, whole, drawing breath after breath. They had grown up with Krishna — had watched him graze the calves, had scolded him and loved him as their own — but they had never seen anything like this. What kind of boy was it whose foot could turn a devouring serpent into a shining god?

They finished their vow in the forest of Ambika as the sun rose, and on the road back to Vraja they told the story at every village they passed. Each telling made it more wonderful, and each telling left them more certain: the boy who walked with them was not merely a boy, and the night in the Ambika forest was only the beginning of what they would see.
reflection: The curse the sages laid on Sudarshana had been a grace all along — punishment as a waiting-room for Krishna's touch. The same night reads three ways: terror for Nanda, astonishment for the cowherds, gratitude for the freed Vidyadhara, and all three are held together by one boy's bare foot.
next_story_tease: The serpent gone and the vow fulfilled, Krishna's road was already turning another way — toward Mathura.
hero_scene: A vast serpent coiled around the sleeping Nanda in the moonlit Ambika forest, cowherds pressing smoking firebrands against its scales, while young Krishna steps calmly forward to touch its head with his bare foot.
